title: Year one close: the big lookout
hookLine: the cycle turns on; next year, the rest of the Torah and the prayer book
carry: you kept me alive for this
tomorrow: Year two opens: back in the cycle

cards: There's a moment at the top of a long hike when you stop looking at your feet. For hours it was the next rock, the next root. Then the trail opens onto a ledge, and you turn around.
The parking lot is a speck. The stream you crossed is a thread. The steep part that nearly made you quit is just a fold in the hill.
You walked all that. Jewish tradition has a blessing for a moment like this, a few Hebrew words for simply having arrived.

teach.b: Camp one was first words. Shalom: hello, goodbye and peace. The Shema, six words.
Shabbat, rest built into the week. A bracha before eating. Tzedakah, giving, from the same root as justice.

Teshuvah, return. Camp two, the stories: the world made and called good, Abraham arguing with God about Sodom, Jacob limping away renamed, Joseph, the sea, Sinai, and a portable tabernacle built from the people's gifts.

teach.h: CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES.
teach.b: Camp three, the practices: holy time instead of holy place, blessings through the day, the holidays as they came, tefillin, kashrut, and study as prayer.

teach.h: CAMPS FOUR AND FIVE: PORTIONS, DEPTHS.
teach.b: Camp four read the weekly portion closely, fourteen portions from Bereshit to Va'era, and stopped at hail with fire flashing inside it.
Camp five went underneath: the sayings of the sages in Pirkei Avot, a taste of Talmud, Hasidic tales, and the Psalms, ending with neshamah, breath and soul. Now the blessing.
It's Shehecheyanu, and the Mishnah already knows it: someone who builds a new house or buys new things says it.
Today many Jews say it on the first night of a festival, over the first fruit of a season, for new clothes, for a baby, for a milestone.
In English it blesses God who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this season. No achievement required.

teach.h: YOU KEPT ME ALIVE FOR THIS.
teach.b: You didn't have to climb well. You only had to arrive. And there's no finish line: when the Torah's last word is read, its first is read right after.
Next year picks up at the hail, reads the Torah to its last word, and opens the prayer book page by page.

how: Many Jews say the Shehecheyanu blessing on the first night of a festival, over the first fruit of a season, for new clothes or a new home, and at personal milestones, thanking God for bringing them to this moment.

o: a blessing said only after a big success
a blessing for having reached a new moment
a prayer of thanks after finishing the Torah

games.q: which camp was it — tap the pairs.
p: the stories, Genesis to the tabernacle

s: Shehecheyanu is only said after a great achievement
it's said simply for arriving: a festival, a first fruit, new clothes, a milestone.
the Mishnah already mentions saying it over a new house
someone who builds a new house or buys new things says it.
when the Torah's last word is read, the reading stops for a season
the first word is read right after. the cycle turns on.

games.q: you've reached something new: the first night of a festival, the first fruit of the season, the end of a long year. what does the tradition do?
o: wait until you've earned it, then celebrate.
say a blessing for simply having arrived.
stay quiet, so as not to jinx it.
games.why: Shehecheyanu: blessing God who kept us alive, sustained us and brought us to this season. arriving is enough.

practice: Let the year pass in front of you like the view from the ledge, and don't grade it: wholehearted days and half-asleep days both led here.
If you pray, say Shehecheyanu now, in Hebrew or in English, for having reached this day; if you don't, quietly name one thing that carried you here, a person, a habit, plain stubbornness.
Then let the thanks sit in your chest for a while.

wordCard.voice: Shehecheyanu. Who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this season — the blessing for simply having arrived, no achievement required.

orig.note: Hebrew: who has kept us alive, the key word of the blessing for arriving.

carryVoice: Your line: you kept me alive for this. Tomorrow the scroll keeps rolling. See you in year two.
